facility_name: City of Morro Bay Water Reclamation Facility
queries: [Page 96] 2.1. Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The Discharger owns and will operate the Facility, which will provide municipal and industrial wastewater services to a population of approximately 10,600 people in the City of Morro Bay. The Facility construction includes infrastructure, pipelines, and appurtenances for influent, effluent, and recycled water. 2.1.1. Membrane Bioreactor (MBR) System Raw wastewater will be conveyed to the Facility headworks, which will include two coarse screen and grit removal trains, a SAFE system box, and two parallel fine screens. Screenings and grit from the headworks facilities will be hauled offsite for disposal. Screened effluent and return activated sludge will flow into two biological nutrient removal (BNR) basins and then pumped to the MBR. The BNR-MBR basins will be configured as two parallel activated sludge treatment trains, each consisting of pre-anoxic, aerobic, and post-anoxic basins in-series. Filtrate from the MBR will be stored in two RO feed tanks, which will provide water for onsite uses and feed water to the RO system which produces water for IPR. Overflows from these tanks will be discharged to an outfall balancing tank. Tertiary treated effluent from the outfall balancing tank will be pumped through an outfall disinfection chlorine contact pipeline and will then be dechlorinated by sodium bisulfite injection prior to discharge through the ocean outfall. 2.1.2. chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.citation: Khan, SJ et al. (2013). Impact of nitrogen loading rates on treatment performance of domestic wastewater and fouling propensity in submerged membrane bioreactor (MBR). BIORESOURCE TECHNOL.
chunks.text: New and stringent wastewater effluent discharge standards have necessitated the use of membrane bioreactors (MBRs), which is the most promising and reliable technology for wastewater treatment and reuse (Huang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008) . The expected annual growth rate for global market of MBR is 10.5%, and it is increasing in value from 296.0 million dollars in 2008 to 488.0 million dollars by 2013 but growth rates of MBR systems are not the same for all world regions (Kraume and Drews, 2010) . Because of the high quality treated effluents produced by MBRs, they are being considered a future replacement for conventional activated sludge systems especially in those re-gions of the world where water scarcity problems force to increase the reuse of high quality treated wastewater (Bolzonella et al., 2010) . Although the capital and energy costs of MBR has been reduced but fouling which is major problem for MBRs exists as a black box due to the complex nature of fouling layers (Meng et al., 2010) .

chunks.citation: Jasper, JT et al. (2017). Toxic Byproduct Formation during Electrochemical Treatment of Latrine Wastewater. ENVIRON SCI TECHNOL.
chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: Although concentrations of lesser chlorinated ethenes were not measured during this trial, the absence of prolonged DCE accumulation in the bioreactor system indicated that dechlorination progressed beyond the DCE level. Overall, stable TCE removal rates >90% were demonstrated by both R1 and R3 at all influent TCE concentrations, with effluent TCE concentrations frequently below the detectable limit (10 lg l À1 ; Table 1 ). These results are comparable with previous studies of the treatment of chlorinated alkenes, which reported efficient removal of tetrachloroethene (PCE) up to concentrations of 50 mg l À1 in an upflow anaerobic sludge bed bioreactor, operated at room temperature (Prakash and Gupta, 2000) , and 98% PCE removal using an anaerobic attached film expanded bed (AA-FEB) process operating at low temperature, but only up to a loading rate of 12 mg l À1 (Carter and Jewell, 2003) .

chunks.text: UV fluence-response curve data were collected by portioning pre-UV wastewater into a petri dish to a depth of 1 cm. Wastewater samples were then exposed to UV fluences between 10 and 60 mJ/cm 2 . Following treatment, samples were enumerated for E. coli and total coliforms. Pre-and post-UV exposure samples collected at the wastewater treatment facility were also enumerated as controls. All samples were collected as singlets per event and processed under subdued red light to reduce the effects of photo-reactivation.

chunks.text: The polymers in wastewater treatment processes are mainly used for the initial sludge treatment and dewatering processes during the treatment and disposal of sewage sludge. However, many WWTPs support the process of biological sludge flocculation in the bioreactor stage, supporting sedimentation and separation of sludge and treated wastewater. The research allowed us to determine the influence of the two applied polymers on the wastewater treatment process in large doses and for extended periods. Additionally, the effect of the polymers on the morphology and activity of activated sludge in wastewater treatment was increased by operating the system in several cycles a day (batch reactor system). The polymers used in the experiments showed various efficiency and dynamics of the flocculation process of activated sludge flocs. A Praestol dose of 5 mg/l allowed complete sludge sedimentation within 2-3 min and reduced SVI by 42 %. chunks.text: The MBR investigated in the study operated in pre-denitrification mode and was already described in detail by Gómez-Silván et al. (2014) . It consisted of an aerated bioreactor (19.4 m 3 ), an anoxic bioreactor (6.8 m 3 ), and a filtration tank (2 m 3 ) comprising three polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) hollow-fiber ultrafiltration membrane modules (0.034 μm nominal pore size, GE Water & Process Technologies, Fairfield, USA). Part of the treated water was retained in a fourth tank (0.2 m 3 ) and used for the periodic backwashing of the membrane modules. The MBR was installed at the facilities of EDAR Sur-WWTP (EMASAGRA, Granada, Spain) and received urban wastewater from the pretreatment unit of the municipal plant, after being filtered through a 1-mm brush screen, as recommended by the membrane manufacturer. Air was supplied to the aerated bioreactor with a fine bubble membrane diffuser and the dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration was maintained automatically in the 0.5-1.6 mg/L range.

chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process.
